title: may and might 1
subtitle: He may be / He might have been
summary: Use may and might to say that something is possible now (may be) or was possible in the past (may have been), and know how they differ from couldn't.

lesson.heading: may / might = perhaps
lesson.text: You are looking for Ben. Nobody is sure where he is, but you get some suggestions. We use **may** or **might** to say that something is possible. You can use may or might - the meaning is the same. The negative forms are **may not** and **might not**.

examples.note: = perhaps he is in his office

examples.text: It **may be** true. or It **might be** true.
It **may not be** true. / She **might not know**.
examples.note: = perhaps it isn't true / perhaps she doesn't know

lesson.heading: may be or maybe?
lesson.text: Note the difference between **may be** (two words: may + verb) and **maybe** (one word = it's possible, perhaps).

lesson.heading: The past: may have / might have
lesson.text: For the past we use **may have ...** or **might have ...** (+ past participle). The negative is may not have / might not have.

examples.text: *A:* I wonder why Kate didn't answer her phone. *B:* She **may have been** asleep.
*A:* I can't find my phone anywhere. *B:* You **might have left** it at work.
examples.note: = perhaps you left it at work

examples.text: *A:* Why wasn't Amy at the meeting yesterday? *B:* She **might not have known** about it.
*A:* I wonder why David was in such a bad mood yesterday. *B:* He **may not have been feeling** well.

lesson.heading: The structure: may / might (not) have + ...
rows: He **may not have been feeling** well.
You **might have left** it at work.

lesson.heading: could is similar - but couldn't is different

left.label: could = it is possible
left.text: Could means the same as may / might.
examples: It's a strange story, but it **could be** true. (= it is possible that it's true)
You **could have left** your phone at work. (= it's possible that you left it there)

right.label: couldn't = it is not possible
right.text: Couldn't is different from may not and might not.
examples: Sarah **couldn't have received** my message. Otherwise she would have replied. (= it is not possible that she got my message)
Why hasn't Sarah replied to my message? I suppose she **might not have received** it. (= it's possible that she didn't receive it - perhaps she did, perhaps she didn't)

lesson.text: might not = 'perhaps not'; couldn't = 'definitely not'. If you are sure something was impossible, use couldn't have, not might not have.

exercises.prompt: Match each question with the reply that fits it.

pairs.left: Is there a bookshop near here?
pairs.right: I'm not sure, but ask Anna. She might know.
I don't know. They might be Brazilian.

pairs.left: I hope you can help me.
pairs.right: I'll try, but it may not be possible.

pairs.left: Why doesn't George answer his phone?
Do you know anyone who has a key to this cupboard?
pairs.right: Rachel might have one, but I'm not sure.

pairs.left: Gary is in a strange mood today.
pairs.right: Yes, he is. He may not be feeling well.

exercises.prompt: A: Whose phone is this? B: It's not mine. It ___.
exercises.explanation: A present possibility: may be / might be (= perhaps it is Tom's).
Maybe (one word) means perhaps. May be (two words) is may + the verb be and needs a subject.

exercises.prompt: Is the speaker talking about now or about the past?

items.text: You might have left it at work.
He may not have been feeling well.

exercises.prompt: A: Gary said he would meet us in the cafe, but he isn't here. B: He might ___ outside. I'll go and look.
exercises.explanation: Something possibly happening now: might be + -ing.

exercises.prompt: A: Who was the guy we saw with Anna yesterday? B: I'm not sure. It may ___ her brother.
exercises.explanation: Yesterday is past, so: may have been (= perhaps it was).

exercises.prompt: A: Is Ellie here? B: I can't see her. She may not ___ yet.
exercises.explanation: Perhaps she hasn't arrived: may not have + past participle.

exercises.prompt: A: I rang Dan's doorbell, but he didn't answer. I'm sure he was there. B: He might not ___ the doorbell.
exercises.explanation: A past possibility in the negative: might not have heard (= perhaps he didn't hear).

exercises.prompt: A: The man you spoke to - are you sure he was American? B: No, I'm not sure. ... Put the words in order to complete B's reply.
exercises.answer: He might not have been American.
exercises.explanation: Perhaps he wasn't American: might not have been.

exercises.prompt: A: I wonder why Tom didn't come to the party. Perhaps he didn't want to come. B: It's possible. He ___ to come.
exercises.explanation: It's possible, but not certain, that he didn't want to come: might not have wanted.

exercises.prompt: A: I wonder how the fire started. Was it an accident? B: No, the police say it ___ an accident. It was deliberate.
exercises.explanation: The police are sure it was not an accident, so it is not possible: couldn't have been.

exercises.statement: Mike says he tried to find you yesterday. - Well, he might not have tried very hard. I was in my office all day.
exercises.explanation: He couldn't have tried very hard. I was in my office all day, so it is not possible that he tried hard. Might not = perhaps not; couldn't = not possible.
